analysis.one_liner: Bans paying lower wages to jobs dominated by women or racial minorities when the work is equivalent in skill, effort, and responsibility.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 10 Democratic cosponsors, never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Pay Act would have amended the Fair Labor Standards Act to bar employers from paying lower wages in jobs dominated by women, racial minorities, or particular national-origin groups when those jobs are equivalent—dissimilar, perhaps, but equal in skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions. Current law only requires equal pay for 'equal work,' so workers in female- or minority-dominated occupations have no claim even when the work is comparably demanding. The bill added anti-retaliation protections (including for discussing wages), class actions, expert fees, compensatory and punitive damages, and EEOC reporting of pay by race, sex, and national origin, while preserving seniority, merit, and business-justification defenses. It was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and people of color working in jobs dominated by their group—custodial, care, clerical, and service work among them—would gain a legal claim when their pay for an equivalent job trails pay in male- or white-dominated jobs. The bill's findings cited a 77-cents-per-dollar gap and estimated that 41 percent of the pay gap is unexplained by education, experience, or other measured factors. Workers who discuss wages would gain explicit protection from retaliation, and prevailing plaintiffs could recover expert fees and sue as a class.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and minority workers in underpaid job categories

how_it_helps.text: It extends the equal-pay principle beyond 'equal work' to 'equivalent jobs'—jobs that may be dissimilar but whose skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions are equivalent—so workers in female- or minority-dominated occupations could challenge lower pay for comparably demanding work.
It lets workers sue as a class, recover expert- witness fees, and win compensatory or punitive damages, making a lawsuit financially realistic for an individual worker.
It makes it unlawful for an employer to fire or punish an employee for asking about, disclosing, or discussing coworkers' wages, protecting the people most likely to uncover a pay gap.

It requires larger employers (25+ at first, 15+ later) to report wage rates by job classification along with employees' sex, race, and national origin, giving regulators and the public the data to see where pay gaps exist.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost: documenting and defending pay differentials, submitting EEOC wage reports by sex, race, and national origin once they reach the size thresholds, and paying damages, expert fees, and legal costs when they lose suits, including class actions. Employers who cannot demonstrate a job-related reason for a pay gap would have to raise wages in the underpaid job, since the bill bars compliance by cutting anyone's pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing pay-equity lawsuits and reporting duties

drawbacks.text: Requiring employers to prove that pay differences between dissimilar but 'equivalent' jobs are job-related or serve a legitimate business purpose would shift a substantial evidentiary burden onto employers, who argue it invites litigation over hard-to-compare positions and could expose them to class-action liability and punitive damages (the bill allows both).

The EEOC would have to define which jobs are 'dominated' by a given sex, race, or national origin and mandate detailed wage reporting by race, sex, and national origin for employers with as few as 15 employees after two years—an administrative burden on employers, especially small and mid-sized businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—giving workers a legal tool to challenge pay gaps between jobs of comparable skill—was real, and the bill included employer protections (seniority, merit, and business-justification defenses, a ban on lowering wages to comply, and small-employer phase-ins). The costs are administrative compliance for employers and litigation risk, and critics argue the "equivalent jobs" standard invites litigation over hard-to-compare jobs. The bill never received a committee hearing or vote, so Congress never weighed these tradeoffs on the record; the outcome simply preserved the existing pay structure.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Introduced January 29, 2013, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions that same day.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point in the two-year Congress.
No version of the bill was ever reported out of committee, so it never appeared on the Senate calendar and the full chamber never voted on it.
With the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015, the bill died; it would have to be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers whose pay practices could have been challenged under an 'equivalent jobs' standard, who bear no new compliance costs, reporting duties, or litigation exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who keep existing pay structures

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator (IA), bill sponsor and chairman of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; despite chairing the committee of referral, the bill never advanced to a hearing or vote.

for.name: 10 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors (Leahy, Boxer, Murray, Lautenberg, Brown, Blumenthal, Gillibrand, and others)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 10 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote to send it to the floor.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate minority (45 of 100 seats in the 113th Congress)
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the all-Democratic sponsorship list signaled the legislation had no path to the 60 votes most major bills need to clear a Senate filibuster.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Employers (all covered industries, especially those with segregated workforces)
industries.note: The bill would have allowed workers to challenge pay gaps between jobs of equivalent skill even across occupations, and exposed employers to class actions, damages, and EEOC wage reporting. Inaction costs employers nothing.
Class actions with expert fees, compensatory and punitive damages, and fee-shifting would have expanded demand for employment-discrimination litigation. With the bill dead, this growth never occurs.
